messages.author: 01f32dcbb5507b45
messages.subject: abundance induced detection
parts:
Hi to all the people again,

I wish to ask you for some opinions-advice in the analysis of some
data. I'm now working on searching and studying snakes in central
Spain, in Mediterranean habitats, and as all of you securily know they
are secretive and difficult to survey, but particularly to obtain
population estimates.
The scarce works I've read uses long-term mark-recapture data to
estimate such parameters, but unfortunately I've not enough funds to
do this long-term research. The fieldwork should be restricted to some
months.

The question is, can I use the abundance induced detectability model
to confidently estimate abundance? It will result in adequate
estimations? At least, could it be used to compare abundances in
different habitats?

My main concern is that the model is based on repeated detection/not
detection data, but when I detect the species it is common that I
found more than one snake. Moreover, in repeated surveys I've found 1,
2 and even 7 snakes in the same places.

Any suggestion or commentary will be welcomed. Many thanks

Pablo

messages.author: 681fb59733e01a1e
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] abundance induced detection
parts:
hi Pablo,
 
 I don't see any reason why you could not apply these methods except perhaps that the underlying distribution of N might not be well approximated by a Poisson distribution and unless you have quite a bit of data estimates can be pretty unstable with a negative binomial model.

 the other issue is that estimates of N from those models do not easily translate into density estimates. That said, if you are surveying areas that are large relative to animal home range size then maybe you could do that in a pretty loose sense.

 The fact that you are obtaining counts of individuals should almost certainly be useful for building more useful models although I gather from your description of the problem that detection of individual snakes is not independent.  That could probably be dealt with somehow.

 Finally, you might try some other methods for surveying snakes such as using distance sampling along transects, using 2 observers to obtain individual encounter history data, or even do some kind of spatial mapping of detections in order to devise territory level encounter histories.

regards
andy

parts:
Hi,

many thanks for the two comments. Well, my research needs involves a robust estimation of abundance or a robust "abundance" value allowing me to compare between two or more habitats.  The main problem was empashized in the first e-mail, due to particular biological and ecological attributes extensive long-term capture-recapture is needed. This sort of work is nowadays impossible.

I will try to explain the one-day fieldwork procedures, that could be repeated several times in the same place. First, I select a surveying place where two people go to work. There each one survey an independent area during about 3-5 hours. Some of the snakes are found active in the ground (or maybe thermorregulating), but they are mostly caugth when founded under stones. I've both detected/not detected data and the number of different individuals seen during the work. The problem is that I'm concerned about how to calculate any index because, as an example one day we found out 1 snake, but three days later we caugth 7 snakes using the same effort. For us, it looks like the animals are hide in the subterranean pathways of voles -abundant in our study sites- and then remains undetected.

Distance sampling is not a valid approach, since I did not think that detectability depends upon distance from oberserver. Further, we did'nt make transect, rather we survey the complete areas (i. e., we cover all the surface and remove any stone). Other potential method, the repeatedcapture-per-unit-effort until we can calculate the regression line is unsuitable because reasons as the previously described, with the same effort the first day we found 1 snake, but the second day we found 7. Therefore, I came to the RN model that it seems to me to be a good starting point or a way to calculate an abundance parameter suited to be comapred among sites.

Perhaps, can I calculate the detectability in each survey site and compare its value? Any prefered procedure if doing this?

Many thanks again,

Pablo

messages.author: 527e14923215b7e4
messages.subject: RE: [unmarked] abundance induced detection
parts:
Hi Pablo,

You raise many important issues that cannot be fully answered in a short email, but here are a few suggestions. It sounds to me that you are using an "area search" method that would lend itself to quadrat sampling. You could put a grid down over your study area and randomly sample a large number of grid cells (or possibly stratify by habitat type). Let's call these plots. All the abundance models in unmarked assume that each plot has a particular number of snakes associate with it (N_i).  The collection of N_i is assumed to follow some distribution such as the Poisson whose mean can be modeled as a function of habitat variables. If you could perfectly observe N_i, then some sort of generalized linear model would suffice. But since you cannot, you need to estimate the probability of detection. To do that, most models in unmarked require that you collect replicate observations at each plot during a time when the N_i does not change (the population is closed). Suppose that you think the population is closed during a 5 day period. You could survey each plot once/day and then use the N-mixture model of Royle (Biometrics 2004) to estimate total population size and test for differences among habitat types.

The closure assumption can be hard to meet. If this is the case, one option would be to use conduct replicate surveys over a very short time period. Perhaps you could survey each plot 3 times/day, or better yet, use removal sampling. For instance, you could search each plot for 10 minutes or so and put each snake in a bag. Then immediately search it again for 10 minutes and continue to bag snakes. Repeat this several consecutive times. If you do this once per plot, you could use the multinomPois() function in unmarked to estimate population size and model variation in abundance.

However, some of the snakes at your plot will not be available for detection since they hang out underground. So, you could do muliptle removal surveys at each plot. Perhaps once/day for 5 days. Then you could use the "gmultmix" function to estimate both the probability of detection and the probability of being available for detection. We just published a paper about this model. http://www.esajournals.org/doi/pdf/10.1890/10-2433.1. The example on the help page shows a similar type of data structure.

Just a suggestion. Hope it helps.

Richard

Richard Chandler, post-doc
USGS Patuxent Wildlife Research Center

messages.author: 20119867e986c754
messages.subject: Re: abundance induced detection
parts:
Hello Pablo-

I thought I would chime in with my comments, but keep in mind I'm a
herpetologist, not a biometrician.

I think you should consider trying to sample in such a way that is
valid to use make the use of the N-mixture model of Royle (2004).
This sounds to me like an appropriate way for you to sample within
your constraints and get useful abundance data that you can report.

There are some good examples of this model being used in the
literature, and it is available as part of unmarked using the pcount()
model-fitting function.

Check out Dodd and Dorazio (2004) for a herp example of this model and
also Kery et al. (2005) with birds. Also, if you are willing to go
Bayesian this model is easily written in WinBUGS. See Royle et al.
(2007) and Kery and Royle (2010).

Hope this helps.

Dodd, C. K., Jr. and R. M. Dorazio. 2004. Using counts to
simultaneously mestimate abundance and detection probabilities in a
salamander community. Herpetologica 60:468-478.
Kery, M. and J. A. Royle. 2010. Hierarchical modelling and estimation
of abundance and population trends in metapopulation designs. Journal
of Animal Ecology 79:453-461.
Kery, M., J. A. Royle, and H. Schmid. 2005. Modeling avian abundance
from replicated counts using binomial misture models. Ecological
Applications 15:1450-1461.
Royle, J. A. 2004. N-mixture models for estimating population size
from spatially replicated counts. Biometrics 60:108-115.
Royle, J. A., M. Kery, R. Gautier, and H. Schmid. 2007. Hierarchical
spatial models of abundance and occurrence from imperfect survey data.
Ecological Monographs 77:465-481.

parts:
Hi,

many thanks for all the comments, these advices were really useful for me. It looks like the N-mixture model is an adequate way to perform the analyses.
May can I make another question to add complexity? As a part of my work, I should also remove the snakes from the field to maintain them under enclosure conditions (for experimental behavioral ecology studies), and I think this kind of data -number removed- is of great help in helping to estimate abundance. Again the common method is the capture-per-unit-effort but I've the same biases I've described in previous e-mails. Any idea or suggestion on how to use this kind of data?

Many thanks again, I don't know how to pay all of you for the advising,

Pablo

messages.author: 527e14923215b7e4
messages.subject: RE: [unmarked] Re: abundance induced detection
parts:
Hi Pablo,

When fitting a removal model with "gmultmix", removals *among* primary sampling periods must be temporary not permanent. For example, you could remove snakes during 3 consecutive 5-minute periods, but then you would need to release them before conducting another round of removals at that plot. Or, if you use only 1 primary period, you do not need to release the snakes, but it will not be possible to estimate the probability of being available for detection.

Richard

> On May 25, 7:26 am, Richard Chandler <rchand...@usgs.gov> wrote:
> > Hi Pablo,
> >
> > You raise many important issues that cannot be fully answered in a short
> > email, but here are a few suggestions. It sounds to me that you are using
> > an "area search" method that would lend itself to quadrat sampling. You
> > could put a grid down over your study area and randomly sample a large
> > number of grid cells (or possibly stratify by habitat type). Let's call
> > these plots. All the abundance models in unmarked assume that each plot
> > has a particular number of snakes associate with it (N_i).  The collection
> > of N_i is assumed to follow some distribution such as the Poisson whose
> > mean can be modeled as a function of habitat variables. If you could
> > perfectly observe N_i, then some sort of generalized linear model would
> > suffice. But since you cannot, you need to estimate the probability of
> > detection. To do that, most models in unmarked require that you collect
> > replicate observations at each plot during a time when the N_i does not
> > change (the population is closed). Suppose that you think the population
> > is closed during a 5 day period. You could survey each plot once/day and
> > then use the N-mixture model of Royle (Biometrics 2004) to estimate total
> > population size and test for differences among habitat types.
> >
> > The closure assumption can be hard to meet. If this is the case, one
> > option would be to use conduct replicate surveys over a very short time
> > period. Perhaps you could survey each plot 3 times/day, or better yet, use
> > removal sampling. For instance, you could search each plot for 10 minutes
> > or so and put each snake in a bag. Then immediately search it again for 10
> > minutes and continue to bag snakes. Repeat this several consecutive times.
> > If you do this once per plot, you could use the multinomPois() function in
> > unmarked to estimate population size and model variation in abundance.
> >
> > However, some of the snakes at your plot will not be available for
> > detection since they hang out underground. So, you could do muliptle
> > removal surveys at each plot. Perhaps once/day for 5 days. Then you could
> > use the "gmultmix" function to estimate both the probability of detection
> > and the probability of being available for detection. We just published a
> > paper about this model.http://www.esajournals.org/doi/pdf/10.1890/10-2433.1. The example on the
> > help page shows a similar type of data structure.
> >
> > Just a suggestion. Hope it helps.
> >

> > I don't see any reason why you could not apply these methods except
> > perhaps that the underlying distribution of N might not be well
> > approximated by a Poisson distribution and unless you have quite a bit of
> > data estimates can be pretty unstable with a negative binomial model.
> >
> > the other issue is that estimates of N from those models do not easily
> > translate into density estimates. That said, if you are surveying areas
> > that are large relative to animal home range size then maybe you could do
> > that in a pretty loose sense.
> >
> > The fact that you are obtaining counts of individuals should almost
> > certainly be useful for building more useful models although I gather from
> > your description of the problem that detection of individual snakes is not
> > independent.  That could probably be dealt with somehow.
> >
> > Finally, you might try some other methods for surveying snakes such as
> > using distance sampling along transects, using 2 observers to obtain
> > individual encounter history data, or even do some kind of spatial mapping
> > of detections in order to devise territory level encounter histories.
